subject: biology

moments.title: Linnaeus publishes Systema Naturae
moments.body:
Carl Linnaeus, a 28-year-old Swedish botanist, publishes the first edition of Systema Naturae — a tabular classification of the three 'kingdoms' (animal, vegetable, mineral). It's 11 pages long.

Over 12 editions, it grows to ~3000 pages. The 10th edition (1758) is the modern starting point for animal nomenclature. Linnaeus introduces binomial nomenclature: every species gets two names (genus and species) — a system still used.
moments.takeaway: A young botanist invents a classification system that lasts for centuries.

moments.title: Apostles and species discovery
moments.body:
Linnaeus sends students (his 'apostles') around the world to collect specimens. Daniel Solander travels with Cook to Australia. Pehr Kalm travels in North America. Several die on their expeditions (Bjornstahl in Cyprus, Forsskal in Yemen, Hasselquist in Smyrna).

The apostles bring back thousands of new species. Linnaeus describes them all in subsequent editions. The number of described species grows rapidly.
moments.takeaway: Biological classification becomes a global enterprise. Apostles pay heavy personal costs for natural history.

moments.title: Darwin gives classification an evolutionary basis
moments.body:
Darwin's On the Origin of Species (1859) reframes taxonomy. Categories are no longer arbitrary divisions — they reflect descent. Species in the same genus share a recent common ancestor; species in the same family a more remote one. Classification becomes phylogenetic.

Darwin: 'Our classifications will come to be, as far as they can be so made, genealogies.'
moments.takeaway: Classification has a biological meaning. Tree-shaped descent maps onto the hierarchical categories.

moments.title: Five kingdoms
moments.body:
Whittaker proposes a five-kingdom system: Monera (bacteria), Protista (single-celled eukaryotes), Fungi, Plantae, Animalia. The system distinguishes prokaryotes from eukaryotes and separates fungi from plants.

Margaret Dayhoff's 1965 molecular sequences begin to provide an alternative classifier — molecular phylogeny. Carl Woese will soon use ribosomal RNA to redraw the deepest branches.
moments.takeaway: Higher-level classification reflects fundamental cellular differences.

moments.title: Woese discovers archaea
moments.body:
Carl Woese sequences 16S ribosomal RNA across many organisms. He finds that some 'bacteria' (methanogens, halophiles, thermoacidophiles) are as different from other bacteria as from eukaryotes. He proposes a third domain: Archaea.

The tree of life now has THREE domains (Bacteria, Archaea, Eukarya) rather than two kingdoms (prokaryote vs eukaryote). Eukaryotes appear most closely related to archaea, especially as nuclear ancestry — consistent with later endosymbiotic theory.
moments.takeaway: Molecular phylogenetics rewrites the deepest divisions of life. Three domains, not two.

now.title: Taxonomy today
now.body:
Molecular phylogenetics dominates. Whole-genome trees, single-gene trees, and metagenomic sequences from environmental samples constantly reshape our view of life.

Most named species (over 1.5 million) are still based on morphology. eDNA and high-throughput sequencing are revealing huge diversity of microbes (CPR bacteria, Asgard archaea — the latter likely the closest archaeal relatives of eukaryotes).
now.open_questions: How many species are there? How do we name species we've only seen as DNA sequences? What were the deepest divergences in the tree of life, and when did they occur? Where do viruses fit (they aren't on the tree in any standard sense)?

reflection: Linnaeus considered humans (Homo sapiens) part of order Primates. This was controversial — he was placing humans in nature, not above it. Two centuries later, Darwin made the connection explicit, and a century after that, DNA showed humans share 98% of their genome with chimps. How has the taxonomic placing of humans alongside other animals shaped — slowly, contentiously — what we think we are?
